title: Three steps in
hook: many step back and then forward before beginning, as if approaching a king

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Amidah, the prayer said on your feet. Your line was standing before. Did you give someone your whole posture? Today, what happens in the two seconds before the standing begins. Day five hundred seventy-four.

A knock on a door that's already open. A pause in the doorway of a boss's office before you step in. People mark entrances even when nothing stands in the way. Before the Amidah, many Jews make one with their feet: three small steps backward, then three small steps forward, ending exactly where they started. If you didn't know, you'd think they'd forgotten something and changed their mind. But it's a whole entrance, compressed into six steps on a carpet. And it borrows its shape from the way people once walked into a throne room.
screen: `A KNOCK ON AN OPEN DOOR.` → `THREE BACK, THREE FORWARD.` → `AN ENTRANCE IN SIX STEPS.`

segments.voice: The steps forward are the older idea. Before you speak to a king, you approach. Commentators point to three moments in the Bible where someone draws near before speaking to God or to power. Abraham draws near to plead for Sodom. Judah draws near to Joseph, the ruler of Egypt, to plead for his brother. Elijah draws near on Mount Carmel before he prays. In the old Jewish translation, Genesis says simply: "And Abraham drew near." Three nearings, three steps. The step backward first is a later custom, and not everyone does it. The idea: you can't walk forward into a presence you're already standing in. So you make a little room, step back, and then come in properly. Halachic codes record the forward steps as a custom many keep. At the end of the Amidah there are three steps back again: the Talmud, in Yoma 53b, compares it to a student taking leave of a teacher, backing away rather than turning around. So the whole prayer sits inside a doorway: three steps in, three steps out. Notice what that does. Prayer doesn't begin when the words begin. It begins when you decide to go in. The steps are a hinge: before them, you're in your day. After them, you're somewhere else, in front of someone. Same carpet. Different room.
screen: `APPROACH BEFORE YOU SPEAK.` · `ABRAHAM, JUDAH, ELIJAH DREW NEAR.` · `STEP BACK TO MAKE ROOM.` · `THREE STEPS IN, THREE STEPS OUT.` · then, large: `THREE STEPS IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take three steps before something important. Think of the next thing today that matters: a call, a meeting, a conversation at dinner, a page you need to write. If you can stand, try it now as a rehearsal. Three small steps back. Pause. Three small steps forward. Feel the shift from wherever you were to where you're about to be. Then sit, breathe, and picture doing it, for real, just before that moment comes. The bell holds the time.
Three steps in. The small entrance many make before the Amidah, approaching as if before a king, with three steps out again at the end.

Your line: three steps in. A week that walked from the Shema's second and third paragraphs, through true and firm and the song at the sea, into no gap, the standing prayer, and its doorway. Today, take three real steps before your important moment. Day five hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Many Jews take three small steps forward before beginning the Amidah, often stepping back first to make room, and at the end take three steps back and bow to each side before stepping forward again; customs on the opening steps vary between communities.
